title: Re'eh: see the choice (Deuteronomy 11:26)
hook: "Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse"

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ger, the stranger, loved because you were strangers once. Your line was love the stranger. Who did you welcome? Today a new portion opens with one word: look. Day four hundred ninety-seven.

Some of the choices that shape a life don't feel like choices while they're being made. Nobody decides to stop calling a brother. It just slowly happens. Nobody chooses two hours of scrolling. They just don't choose not to. Psychologists have names for it: defaults, habits, autopilot. Life comes at you as a stream, and the forks in the road go by without signs. The new portion opens by stopping that stream. Before it says a word about what to choose, it tells you to look.
screen: `CHOICES THAT DON'T FEEL LIKE CHOICES.` → `AUTOPILOT.` → `FIRST, LOOK.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse." The first word, behold, is re'eh in Hebrew. See. It gives the portion its name. And there's a small oddity some commentators point out. Re'eh is singular: see, you, one person. But before you is plural: all of you. A whole people stands there, and each one is told to see for themselves. Nobody can look for you. Then the choice is laid out plainly. The blessing, if you listen to the commandments; the curse, if you turn aside. And Moses gives it a geography. When you cross the Jordan, set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal, two real mountains. Later, in the book of Joshua, the people do exactly that: half of them in front of one mountain, half in front of the other, and the blessing and the curse read aloud. A choice you can stand between and see with your eyes. And then two small words: this day. Not once, at Sinai, settled for good. Today, set before you again. Some Jewish teachers hear in it a basic idea: that a person is free, and the road forks every day. The Torah doesn't pretend the choice is easy, or that it's always obvious. It asks for something earlier and simpler. See it. Notice that there's a fork at all.
screen: `RE'EH: SEE.` · `SEE, YOU. BEFORE ALL OF YOU.` · `GERIZIM AND EBAL.` · `THIS DAY, AGAIN.` · then, large: `SEE THE CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one choice point today. Settle, and breathe. Walk through the rest of your day in your mind, hour by hour. Somewhere in it there's a fork you'd normally slide past without noticing. The first thing you pick up in the morning. What you say when you walk in the door. Whether you answer that message. Find one. Picture the two mountains facing each other there. You don't have to decide now. Just mark the spot, so you'll see it when you get there. The bell holds the time.
Re'eh. See, or behold. Said to one person, in front of everyone: the first word and the name of the portion.

Your line: see the choice. A week that went beyond the letter, lived by more than bread, credited other hands, asked simply, opened the heart, and loved the stranger. Today, when you reach your fork, stop for one breath and see it. Day four hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Re'eh is read in synagogues in late summer, usually around the start of the month of Elul, when the season of reflection and self-examination before the High Holy Days begins.

myth: re'eh is addressed to the whole crowd in the plural
re'eh is singular; before you is plural. each one sees for themselves.
the blessing and curse were tied to two real mountains
Gerizim for the blessing, Ebal for the curse.
the people actually carried out the ceremony later
in the book of Joshua, half the people stood in front of each mountain.

fork.setup: Moses sets a blessing and a curse before the people. before saying what to choose, what's the first thing he asks?
fork.reveal: re'eh: behold, see. the choice starts with noticing that there's a fork at all.

original.note: Hebrew: see, behold. singular, though spoken to all Israel.

trapdoor: what you thought: obey and be blessed, disobey and be cursed.
what it means: first, see. each person, this day, is shown a real fork in the road.
what a scholar hears: re'eh is singular and lifneichem, before you, is plural; Joshua 8 carries out the Gerizim and Ebal ceremony.
